newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs plan to honour indicted war criminal.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs plan to honour indicted war criminal.

text.p: Bosnian Serb authorities planned to honour a notorious police chief as a fallen hero on Sunday, three days after British soldiers shot him dead while trying to arrest him on war crimes charges.
The former police chief of Prijedor, Simo Drljaca, was shot on Thursday after he opened fire on British special forces trying to detain him.
The U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague had charged him with orchestrating a genocidal campaign against Moslems and Croats in the Prijedor region early in the Bosnian war.
His associate, Milan Kovacevic, was nabbed by British troops, also on Thursday, and extradited to The Hague under a sealed indictment.
The United States and European governments praised the unprecedented swoop as a breakthrough for peacemaking efforts in Bosnia.
Nationalist Serb leaders, who also promoted "ethnic cleansing" in wartime, have portrayed Drljaca as an innocent victim who was "murdered".
Authorities said they planned a commemoration for Drljaca in his home town of Prijedor in the morning and a funeral ceremony later in the northwestern town of Banja Luka.
The NATO raid aggravated a power struggle among Bosnian Serbs and the leadership moved to resolve the feud over the weekend.

Seeking to present a united front, Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic and her rival, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, held talks for the first time since their political conflict erupted this month.
The Serbian Orthodox church, which has close links to the ultra-nationalist leadership, helped broker the meeting in Banja Luka.

Patriarch Pavle, the highest church authority, travelled to Bosnia's autonomous Serb republic to help mediate in the confrontation which pits Plavsic against hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

Plavsic dissolved parliament when hardliners tried to sabotage her attempts to expose large-scale corruption. Serb media, controlled by Karadzic loyalists, have accused Plavsic of provoking political turmoil which allowed NATO to strike at the war crimes suspects.
"We have many enemies who want to destroy the Serb republic and we have to be aware of it," Krajisnik told Serb television.
The NATO raid, codenamed "Operation Tango", broke new ground for the alliance-led peacekeeping mission which had previously ruled out going after suspects unless troops happened to stumble upon them.
NATO officers had spoken of the possibility of a violent backlash if suspects were arrested but there were no reprisals or serious threats against peacekeeping troops after the raid.
International police monitors stationed in Serb-controlled territory, who are unarmed, were conducting "business as usual", a spokesman said.
Western diplomats say prosecuting war crimes is a crucial step in building post-war reconciliation and clearing the way for the scheduled withdrawal of NATO troops within a year.

NATO declined to discuss whether there would be more arrests but the raid in Prijedor and the use of sealed indictments raised expectations that more suspects would be seized in Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.
The shift in tactics also fed speculation that the two most prominent suspects on the published list of indictments -- Karadzic and his former army commander General Ratko Mladic -- might be next.
Krajisnik indicated the Serb leadership feared just such an action and said the raid in Prijedor may have been "a test run for something that might happen in the future".
